d: Stationarity, backtesting, metrics, deep and foundation models, and the production questions. Expect a leakage trap.
Design principles, testing, APIs, delivery, architecture and security — the craft questions senior loops use to calibrate level.
Language internals, concurrency, performance and gotchas — expect predict-the-output questions and why.
Trade-offs under load — databases, consistency, messaging, reliability and capacity math. Expect follow-up questions asking why and what breaks.
What happens on the wire — expect 'what happens when…', refused vs timeout, TIME_WAIT, TLS and HTTP-version follow-ups.
Implement one algorithm from scratch in NumPy — the maths, the shapes, a test you can verify by hand, then stability and complexity.

draw.hint: Shapes first, maths in one line, loop version, test it against something you can verify, then vectorise and make it numerically stable. Finish with complexity and the obvious extension.

d: Vision encoders, VLM design, generation, speech and serving — expect token-budget arithmetic and 'how would you build it' follow-ups.
Test-time compute, RL for LLMs, verifiable rewards, reward hacking and evaluation — expect to compute advantages, pass@k and error bars.
Arithmetic intensity, memory and FLOPs arithmetic, kernels, parallelism and serving performance — expect back-of-envelope numbers out loud.

Scheduling and replacement arithmetic, synchronization and deadlock, virtual memory, file systems and I/O, containers and Linux debugging — expect to trace an algorithm by hand and explain what the kernel does.

Normalization and keys, live SQL with joins, NULLs and window functions, B+ tree and LSM arithmetic, reading a query plan, WAL and MVCC traces, and data-modelling trade-offs — expect to write SQL and trace the engine by hand.

Probability and Bayes by hand, distributions and the CLT, MLE and MAP, p-values, power and A/B sample sizes, eigenvectors and the SVD of small matrices, gradients and the chain rule through a small network, Lagrange multipliers, and entropy, cross-entropy and KL: expect to calculate on the whiteboard and explain each result to a non-statistician.

Container internals and Dockerfile review, image supply chain, Kubernetes architecture and the apply-to-running trace, rolling updates, Services and DNS, requests, limits and throttling arithmetic, HPA maths, debugging CrashLoopBackOff and OOMKilled, and GPU scheduling and inference autoscaling.

Designing an eval for an LLM feature, golden-set sizing and confidence intervals by hand, judge bias and validation against humans, kappa from a table, recall@k and nDCG, paired comparisons and sample sizes, A/B tests with implicit feedback, red-team severity, synthetic-data pitfalls, MinHash dedup and decontamination, and CI gates and drift alerts: expect to compute on the whiteboard and defend every number.

Deciding workflow versus agent with the reliability and cost maths, tracing a tool-call episode as message JSON, tool and MCP design, context growth and caching savings by hand, memory and injection defences, graphs with approvals and parallel calls, multi-agent trade-offs, sandbox and trifecta threat models, durable execution and idempotency, agent evals with pass^k and clustered intervals, and a cost model at 100k tasks a day: expect to design on the whiteboard and defend every number.

Sketching the retrieval-ranking-re-ranking funnel with a latency budget and server count, computing BM25, an ALS step, an in-batch softmax loss, RRF, nDCG and MRR by hand, choosing ranking models and losses, debiasing clicks with propensities, Thompson sampling for cold start, diversity and exposure in re-ranking, interleaving versus A/B tests, and placing LLMs where their cost pays: expect to design the feed or search on the whiteboard and defend every number.

Placing authentication and authorisation checks across gateway, service and database, costing password hashes in GPU guesses per second, recomputing a JWT signature and a PKCE challenge by hand, tracing OAuth and OIDC flows and their attacks, computing a TOTP code, answering 'can Alice edit doc 42?' with RBAC and ReBAC, fixing an IDOR with row-level security, designing workload identity and secrets for a fleet, and scoping an agent's delegated token: expect to design auth for a B2B SaaS on the whiteboard and defend every choice.

Evaluating an IAM request with an allow and an explicit deny, planning a three-zone VPC and pricing NAT, cross-zone and egress traffic, choosing between instances, containers and functions with numbers, sizing DynamoDB capacity, picking delivery semantics for a pipeline, reading a Terraform plan that replaces a database, computing RTO and RPO for a DR plan, estimating a monthly bill and a GPU fine-tuning run: expect to design a production AWS architecture on the whiteboard and defend its cost, security and failure behaviour.

Finding the planted bugs in a short training script — unshifted labels, a leaking mask, softmax over the wrong dimension, a double softmax, a broadcast loss, a forgotten eval() — and explaining each symptom; reading strides and views; placing zero_grad, clipping and the scheduler; fixing gradient accumulation and GradScaler order; estimating memory for weights, optimiser state and activations; a correct KV cache; DDP buckets and no_sync versus FSDP2; and removing syncs and graph breaks from a slow loop: expect to debug out loud and defend every fix with a check.

Design a training-data pipeline from CDC to sharded training sets, size a Parquet layout and a Spark join, trace a watermark and an Iceberg commit, debug a job that went from 20 minutes to 4 hours, and cost it on three engines — expect numbers on the whiteboard.

Risk taxonomies, alignment methods, evaluation awareness, interpretability, dangerous-capability evals, frontier frameworks and launch decisions — expect to report papers precisely and reason through a ship-or-hold call.

Pick a north star and guardrails for a feature, turn it into a model objective, diagnose a 10% drop to a root cause, spot the ratio or short-term trap in a scorecard, size an AI feature's value against its cost per query, and make a launch call with conditions: expect numbers on the whiteboard and follow-ups that change one assumption.
Explain how you would recognise and solve problems out loud: pattern choice, invariants, complexity and edge cases.
STAR stories with real numbers. Ownership, conflict, failure, influence.
